about: The guidebook: the principles, concerns, methods, data rules and known limits every finding is cited against, the concern ladder, and the steps of the algorithm with the entries they apply and the tables they need. Each entry states its basis; 'Administration policy' marks a choice the administration owns, not an external rule.

sections.about: How Tosi works, whatever the filing.

sections.about: What makes a filing a concern for the country.

sections.title: Methods
sections.about: How each value is worked out.

sections.about: How doubtful or missing data is treated.

sections.title: Known limits
sections.about: What Tosi does not yet cover, said plainly.

entries.title: No generated facts
entries.rule: Every value comes from a filed record, a published table or a stated formula. No language model or learned model takes part in any result.
entries.why: A concern raised with another country has to survive its engineers checking it. A model can produce a fluent number nobody can trace. A formula can be checked line by line.
entries.effect: Every line in a brief expands back to a table row, a limit or a formula.

entries.title: Same input, same result
entries.rule: Rerunning the same files gives the same findings, and every result records the fingerprints of its inputs.
entries.why: If two runs disagree, nobody knows which to trust. Fingerprints also prove which file a result came from, long after the fact.
entries.effect: Reruns are compared byte by byte, and each result records the hashes of its inputs.

entries.title: People decide
entries.rule: The system proposes and shows its evidence. An expert decides, and nothing is sent automatically.
entries.why: Coordination is a judgement between administrations. Software can find and measure, but it can't carry that responsibility.
entries.effect: Letters are always drafts, and the system stops at the expert.

entries.title: Secondary review stays outside results
entries.rule: AI review may run separately to look for anything missed. Its output is a list of suggestions for people. It cannot create, change or rank a finding.
entries.why: Rules only catch what someone thought to write down, so a separate review can find gaps. That review can also be wrong, so it must never touch a result directly.
entries.effect: A suggestion goes on a review list. It only matters once a person accepts it as a new or changed rule.

entries.title: Rules change by review
entries.rule: A rule changes only as a proposal that is tested on past issues, approved by a person and given a new guidebook version. Nothing rewrites live rules on its own.
entries.why: Regulations and data change, so rules must change too. But a rule that changes silently would make old and new results impossible to compare.
entries.effect: Each change is tested on past issues first, so its effect on real findings is visible before anyone approves it.

entries.title: What counts as a concern
entries.rule: An exceedance of the applicable limit is a concern. So is a result close to the limit, or a high level close to a protected frequency.
entries.why: A limit is pass or fail, but interference isn't. A filing just under a limit is one small modification from breaching it, and a strong signal just outside a Finnish band can still reach a receiver. So the net is wider than the hard limit.
entries.effect: Cases are placed on the concern ladder, with clear exceedances at the top and near misses below them.

entries.title: Near-limit margin
entries.rule: A result within 3 dB of the limit is treated as near the limit.
entries.why: 3 dB is a factor of two in power. Filings get modified, and every calculation carries some uncertainty, so a result this close shouldn't be treated as safely clear.
entries.effect: This value is a choice, not a regulation, so it can be changed in one place and its effect tested.

entries.title: High-gain receivers in line with a source
entries.rule: The trigger is lowered by 6 dB for a directional station of at least 20 dBi whose beam includes a geostationary source.
entries.why: A high-gain antenna collects far more energy from where it points. A satellite sitting in that beam can cause harm even when its PFD is within the limit. Geostationary satellites stay in one place, so this can be worked out exactly.
entries.effect: The angle from each directional station to the satellite is compared with the antenna's beamwidth. Moving satellites aren't tested, because they don't stay in any beam.

entries.title: What is protected
entries.rule: Receive frequencies are protected. Transmit frequencies are protected too, because every transmission is received somewhere in Finland. Broadcasting is protected across its coverage area.
entries.why: Finnish use isn't only where a receiver is listed. Radio listeners, television viewers and the far end of a radio link are all receivers, even when the register lists just the transmitter.
entries.effect: A station is matched on both its receive and transmit frequencies.

entries.title: Worst case for satellites
entries.rule: PFD is calculated with peak antenna gain toward Finland, whatever the filed beam. The result is a ceiling, not a prediction.
entries.why: Public filings don't reliably say where a beam points, and satellites can change their pointing. Assuming the peak lands on Finland can raise a false alarm, but it won't hide a real problem.
entries.effect: A filing that passes here passes anywhere. One that fails may still be fine, so an expert looks at it.

entries.title: PFD limits
entries.rule: Limits, bands and arrival-angle masks are those of the Radio Regulations, as held in the ITU BR PFD tables.
entries.why: These limits are agreed internationally, and taking them from ITU's own tables avoids copying errors. They vary with arrival angle because ground antennas look at the horizon, so low-angle signals do more harm.
entries.effect: The limit is evaluated at the angle that gives the smallest margin.

entries.title: Power in the reference bandwidth
entries.rule: Filed power is converted to the limit's reference bandwidth by the rule in the technical annex.
entries.why: Limits are stated per 4 kHz or per 1 MHz, but filings give total power or a density. Without conversion the two numbers aren't comparable.
entries.effect: The filed power is converted first, then compared.

entries.title: Land-mobile scope
entries.rule: Terrestrial screening covers base stations (FB) and land mobile stations (ML).
entries.why: The coordination threshold was written for land-mobile systems. Applying it to other services would give numbers that look exact but mean little.
entries.effect: Fixed and other services are left out of this screening, and the reason is recorded.

entries.title: Propagation
entries.rule: Field strength uses P.1546-6 at 10% time and 50% locations with a 10 m receiving height, without a terrain profile.
entries.why: Near the ground, radio doesn't follow a simple distance law. P.1546 is the agreed statistical model. The 10% time figure captures the occasional strong conditions that actually cause interference.
entries.effect: The model is run for each border point, using the filed power and height.

entries.title: Coordination threshold
entries.rule: The trigger field strength is the T/R 25-08 value for the band, with its bandwidth correction.
entries.why: This is the European trigger level. Below it, neighbours don't need to coordinate. The correction allows for wider channels, which pick up more power.
entries.effect: The calculated field is compared with the threshold for that band.

entries.title: Above 470 MHz
entries.rule: Above 470 MHz, the T/R 25-08 value for above 400 MHz is applied.
entries.why: The recommendation stops at 470 MHz, yet many land-mobile filings are higher. Extending the last value gives a consistent test instead of no test.
entries.effect: Results above 470 MHz are labelled, so a reviewer knows the rule was extended.

entries.title: Where field strength is assessed
entries.rule: Field strength is assessed at several points on the land borders and the outer limit of the territorial sea, and the highest value is kept. Listed stations sharing the channel are assessed at their own location.
entries.why: The strongest field isn't always at the nearest point, because a path over sea carries further than one over land. Listed stations matter too, since that is where harm would be felt.
entries.effect: Five spaced points are tested per station, and the highest value is kept.

entries.title: When no value can be calculated
entries.rule: A satellite that cannot see Finland is clear. A band with no applicable limit is recorded as such. Only missing data counts as cannot calculate.
entries.why: These are three different facts and shouldn't look alike. A satellite that can't see Finland can't interfere. No limit means the rule doesn't apply. Missing data means we don't know, and a person should look.
entries.effect: Each outcome has its own place on the ladder.

entries.title: Conflicting bandwidths
entries.rule: When channel and transmission bandwidth disagree, the smaller is used.
entries.why: A mismatch is usually a data error. One fixed rule keeps results consistent and stops a typing error from creating false overlaps.
entries.effect: The mismatch is flagged, and the smaller value is used.

entries.title: Missing licence class
entries.rule: A blank class is recorded as other (MUUT). Radio parameters decide the result, not the class.
entries.why: A blank class shouldn't remove a station from protection. What matters is what it transmits and receives.
entries.effect: The station stays in the analysis, recorded as other.

entries.title: Implausible values
entries.rule: Antenna gains above 60 dBi are not used. Stations outside the national outline are kept and flagged.
entries.why: One impossible value shouldn't drive a result. Dropping the value is safer than guessing a replacement.
entries.effect: The station stays in the analysis, and only the bad value is ignored.

entries.title: Territorial-sea limit
entries.rule: The limit is approximated as a 12 nautical mile offset of the coastline, cut at the median line. It is not the official boundary.
entries.why: The official boundary follows baselines that aren't in our data. In places it is narrower than our offset, so results near the sea limit are approximate.
entries.effect: A case that depends on this limit should be checked against the official boundary.

entries.title: Plan appendices
entries.rule: Appendices 30, 30A and 30B are not assessed, because their plans are published outside the IFIC file.
entries.why: These plans have their own rules and are published separately, so a clean result here doesn't cover them.
entries.effect: Filings under these appendices need separate checking for now.

entries.title: Footnote country lists
entries.rule: Limits that apply only to countries listed in a footnote are not applied.
entries.why: Some limits apply only to countries named in a footnote, and those lists aren't fully structured yet.
entries.effect: If Finland is named in such a footnote, the limit won't be applied automatically.

entries.title: Regulation text
entries.rule: Rules are cited by reference. The clause text itself is not shown.
entries.why: A rule is cited by its number, but its wording isn't shown yet.
entries.effect: A reader who needs the exact words has to open the Radio Regulations.
